title: Havana Syndrome: ¿Qué Diablos?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Havana Syndrome, the unexplained cluster of neurological symptoms first reported by US and Canadian diplomats and CIA officers in Havana, Cuba, starting around December 2016. They cover the initial symptoms, the FBI search, the State Department's response and diplomat expulsions, the sonic attack theory and why acoustic experts doubted it (infrasound, ultrasound), the National Academies of Sciences (NASEM) study favoring directed pulsed radio frequency energy and the Frey effect, criticism of that conclusion, the earlier CDC "Cuba Unexplained Events" report, alternative theories (pesticides, microwaves, mass hysteria, conversion disorder), comparable mass psychogenic outbreaks in Portugal, New York and Oklahoma, the Russian microwave history, and the episode's unresolved ending. The episode closes with a listener mail from Abigail.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to Havana syndrome
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the medical mystery of Havana syndrome, note there will be no resolution, and describe the late 2016 onset of symptoms among a CIA station agent in Havana after the US embassy reopened in Cuba.

segments.title: Symptoms and the cluster of cases
segments.summary: Describes the reported symptoms (ear pain, tinnitus, headaches, hearing loss, vertigo, nausea, blurred vision, nosebleeds, fatigue), the range of severity, and the cluster of around ninety cases concentrated in diplomats and CIA officers in Havana and two hotels.

segments.title: FBI investigation and State Department response
segments.summary: The FBI searched the residences and found nothing, the State Department kept the matter quiet, the US and Cuba expelled diplomats, Cuba denied involvement, and Marco Rubio publicly called it a sonic attack.

segments.title: Sonic attack theory and acoustic limits
segments.summary: Explains why acoustic experts doubted a sonic attack: infrasound and ultrasound each have limits, large equipment would be needed, and sound cannot plausibly cause brain damage.

segments.title: Alternative theories and the National Academies study
segments.summary: The hosts describe the investigation's early shortcomings, such as delayed treatment and redacted medical files, and alternative theories including viral attack, pesticide poisoning, microwaves, and mass hysteria.

segments.title: Directed pulsed RF energy and the Frey effect
segments.summary: The NASEM panel favored directed pulsed radio frequency energy and cited the Frey effect, a microwave-induced clicking sound. Critics pointed out a leaked recording and the energy needed would be lethal. A joking tangent about the Eagles and Glenn Frey follows.

segments.title: Psychogenic explanations and past outbreaks
segments.summary: Pesticide and other studies are discussed, including a Ben Gurion University study. The Cuban Academy of Sciences and many scientists favored conversion disorder. Comparable outbreaks in Portugal (2006), New York (2011-12) and Oklahoma (2017) are described.

segments.title: CDC report and case details
segments.summary: The CDC's eighteen-page Cuba Unexplained Events Investigation report, largely unknown to Congress, documented about ninety-five cases, a two-stage illness in fifteen, and identified the first CIA officer who reported symptoms in December 2016.

segments.title: Russia, Cuba, and unresolved debate
segments.summary: Discusses Russian microwave bombardment of the US embassy in Moscow in the 1970s, Cuba's denials and tourism concerns, a brain-scan study and critiques, and the claim that the recorded sound matches a Cuban cricket. The mystery remains unresolved.

segments.title: Listener mail from Abigail
segments.summary: A listener thanks the hosts for the podcast's influence through school, travel and grad school, and the hosts respond.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the contact email and close the episode.
